messages.author: fd4f3538f907404b
messages.subject: Re: Using stat_smooth with other software output
parts:
I think Hadley may have misunderstood (or I'm misunderstanding).

Suppose you have (or can construct) a design matrix X; the
coefficients of
the linear predictor p; and the variance-covariance matrix of the
coefficients V.

Then the predicted values of the linear predictor are LP = X %*% p
" " " " response
plogis(LP) [i.e., inverse-link transform of LP]

The variance of the linear predictor predictions is V_LP = X %*% V
%*% t(X) [I think; play around with
this until it makes sense]
If you want the confidence intervals of the response, you should use

plogis(LP +/- 1.96 * sqrt(V_LP))

if you construct an appropriate data frame with pred, pred_lo,
pred_hi, you can then use geom_line()
to add the prediction and geom_ribbon() [or geom_linerange()] to add the
confidence intervals on the prediction.

Ben Bolker

So this is either a single categorical predictor variable with two
levels or (more likely) a single continuous predictor variable?
I think you'll have to do what I suggested, in this case (since you
have only a single predictor) your design matrix is a column
of 1's (the intercept) plus a column containing the values of the
continuous predictor for which you want predictions.
It's a bit funny that the variances are so close to equal, must be
something special about the model?
The intercept and logit-slope are pretty strongly correlated, you
might want to try centering your predictors ...

This graph doesn't make sense because I have chosen silly ranges for
the predictors, but the general idea should be OK.

coefs <- c(-4.95,0.003,0.755)

vc <- matrix(c(1.16,-0.00028,-0.28,
               -0.00028,-0.0000011,-0.00011,
               -0.28,-0.00011,0.102),
             nrow=3,byrow=TRUE)


library(ggplot2)

## since we have two continuous predictors and want to show
## uncertainty, we're pretty much stuck with a conditioning plot
## i.e., 'slicing' one predictor into discrete categories;
## very hard to construct perspective/contour plots that are actually
## interpretable when we are superimposing either data or confidence
## intervals on the surface

predframe <- expand.grid(x=1:100,y=seq(0,88,length=9))
mm <- cbind(1,as.matrix(predframe)) ## model matrix
pred_eta <- mm %*% coefs
se_pred_eta <- diag(mm %*% tcrossprod(vc,mm))

pred <- plogis(pred_eta)
pred_lo <- plogis(pred_eta-1.96*se_pred_eta)
pred_hi <- plogis(pred_eta+1.96*se_pred_eta)

predframe <- cbind(predframe,yfac=factor(predframe$y),
                   pred,pred_lo,pred_hi)

ggplot(predframe,aes(x=x,y=pred,ymin=pred_lo,ymax=pred_hi))+
  geom_line()+geom_ribbon(alpha=0.5,colour=NA)+
  facet_wrap(~yfac)

OK: this reminds me a bit of 'termplot' or perhaps plot.Predict from the rms package
   Instead of setting up a continuous range of one predictor and a discrete range of
the other predictor, I guess you want to set one predictor to a fixed value and let the others vary.

Something like

predframe <- cbind(
     data.frame(x=1:100,y=mean_y),
     data.frame(x=mean_x,y=1:100))

## use sensible ranges for each variable rather than "1:100"

variable <- rep(c("x","y"), each=100)

construct predictions and standard errors as shown below;
add 'variable' to the data frame; and facet_wrap on 'variable'
with free x scales
